maternal Pb exposure, prenatal stress, and offspring stress, all independently modify the trajectory of neurochemistry in the developing brain, that the direction of the modification can be reversed by environmental manipulations, that the direction and magnitude of the modification depends on gender, and that the direction and extent of modification depends on the brain region.

1) time alone and a behavioral intervention (EM) modified the trajectories of monoamine levels in the frontal cortex, nucleus acumbens and striatal regions of the brains of adult offspring, and 2) Pb and/or stress modified these trajectories in both NEM and EM conditions, but the effects were more pronounced in the NEM condition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effects of environmental conditions on developmental insults and their consequences for behavior.
understanding the mechanisms by which early insults, including those associated with developmental lead exposure, can lead to adaptive and maladaptive behaviors.
understanding how environmental conditions influence developmental insults and their consequences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the trajectory of monoaminergic changes is influenced by the interaction of environmental factors and early life stressors, but that these changes are not necessarily maladaptive.

the effects of developmental Pb and stress are highly dependent on the environmental conditions that follow the insult and that these environmental conditions can either exacerbate or reverse the effects of developmental insults.

time alone and a series of behavioral manipulations typically used as outcome variables in intervention studies can modify the trajectory of neurobiological changes that are induced by Pb exposure or stress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of Pb+/-PS+/-OS can be modified by time alone and EM conditions.

the effects of Pb exposure and/or stress are not fixed at the time of exposure but can change over time and that the direction of these changes is dependent upon the environmental conditions to which the animal is exposed.
the effects of developmental Pb+/- stress are modified by time alone and by EM procedures, but that the latter can fully reverse the former.
The main takeaway from our work is that
environmental conditions, including those used in intervention studies, can modify the outcomes of early insults and that this must be considered in the design of such studies.

it is critical to understand the neurobiological mechanisms that underlie environmental influences on developmental Pb+/-stresses, and the extent to which these can be reversed by behavioral manipulations.
the effects of early insults on behavior and brain function may be modifiable by subsequent experience.
